name: Jean-Jacques Rousseau
description: Political philosopher assessed through popular sovereignty, civic community, education and critiques of inequality.

axes.brief: The sovereign people should enact laws directly, with government acting as a subordinate executor rather than a sovereign representative.
axes.counter: The general will, civil exclusions and gender hierarchy differ from inclusive modern liberal democracy; elected aristocratic government differs from expert rule without popular sovereignty.

axes.brief: Liberty depended on membership in a common self-governing civic order that could enforce common obligations.
axes.counter: His resistance to arbitrary domination coexisted with censorship and coercion in defence of civic commitments; modern privacy safeguards are analogies.

axes.brief: Civic education, shared customs and patriotic attachment were important to sustaining a republic.
axes.counter: Religious toleration was limited by civic loyalty and rejection of intolerance; modern Indigenous and migrant language policies are not directly established.

axes.brief: Small cohesive republics and civic attachment suggest managed settlement rather than an unconditional right to migrate.
axes.counter: His own experience as a displaced outsider does not establish a full immigration programme; family protection and asylum remain qualified estimates.

axes.brief: Republican independence and defence were compatible with scepticism of conquest and militarised prestige.
axes.counter: Citizen military obligations and defensive preparation are more plausible than absolute pacifism; eighteenth-century institutions do not answer autonomous AI targeting.

axes.brief: A people’s general will and sovereignty could not simply be alienated to outside authorities.
axes.counter: Confederal cooperation and peaceful projects could be useful; sovereign republicanism does not imply economic isolation or rejection of all alliances.

axes.brief: Property existed under civic regulation and the common good; economic dependence and concentrated wealth were criticised.
axes.counter: Critique of inequality is not a proposal to nationalise all firms; many modern service-ownership questions lack a direct counterpart.

axes.brief: Economic independence and simplicity suggest domestic resilience with limited external dependence.
axes.counter: These writings do not contain a modern tariff programme; voluntary exchange and pragmatic cooperation qualify broad protection estimates.

axes.brief: Civic authority could regulate economic relations and protect citizens against dependency while ordinary production remained decentralised.
axes.counter: Political sovereignty does not automatically imply compulsory output planning; modern currencies, rent controls and lending instruments are analogical.

axes.brief: A republic should prevent extreme wealth and poverty from undermining equal civic standing.
axes.counter: He favoured preventing concentration and civic dependence rather than an exact modern welfare-state architecture; each tax and benefit mechanism remains an estimate.

axes.brief: Civil religion supported shared civic commitments under the sovereign rather than an autonomous clerical power.
axes.counter: The Social Contract rejected intolerant sectarian domination yet allowed exclusion for rejecting civic religious dogmas; this is neither full secular neutrality nor clerical theocracy.

axes.brief: Education and family roles assigned men and women distinct functions and stressed modesty and domestic virtue.
axes.counter: His critique of corrupt convention challenged some traditions; support for social authenticity does not erase conventional sex and family hierarchy.

axes.brief: Criticised the moral effects of arts, luxury and scientific prestige, favouring simplicity and caution about social development.
axes.counter: He studied botany and invented musical notation; scepticism of civilisation is not blanket rejection of all science or beneficial infrastructure.

axes.brief: Small republics, local civic participation and confederal arrangements could protect self-government.
axes.counter: Each republic’s sovereign authority still constrained municipalities; localism does not imply every council may alter its own boundaries without broader consent.

axes.brief: Perfectibility and social relations transform human conduct; education can cultivate dispositions, while natural self-preservation, pity and sex differences remain.
axes.counter: Natural goodness is not a claim that all observed differences are inherited. Natural compassion and sex-role arguments qualify a uniformly social explanation; racial IQ comparisons lack a direct counterpart.
